analysis.title: Global oil market tracker, Issue 22
key_insights: ANZ classifies the oil market as 'vulnerable' on its resilience dashboard. Stress shows across supply, logistics, inventories and refining, and usable spare capacity is limited.
Persian Gulf crude exports are 14.3mb/d and fell for a fourth consecutive week. Preliminary data point to further declines in late October.
Effective Strait of Hormuz throughput is about 60% of normal and trending lower. Recorded transits are near zero, and dark-fleet traffic is just over two vessels per day.
Surplus OPEC capacity is assessed at 0mb/d under prevailing conditions. Spare production cannot become deliverable supply while export routes are constrained.
Global distillate inventories are 4.9% below the five-year average and diesel cracks are USD103.8/bbl. ANZ reads this as persistent product scarcity and refining system stress.
Yanbu loadings remain low as Houthi attacks on energy infrastructure constrain Red Sea exports.

US crude production fell sharply on hurricane disruption. US crude and fuel exports edged lower, and Strategic Petroleum Reserve draws resumed as the White House reiterated its plan to release the final 40mbbl of the original 172mbbl.
SPR flow rates will stay low because of technical challenges extracting oil from nearly depleted storage.
Crude inventories declined across all regions, led by a sharp fall in the Middle East. Global product stocks edged lower.
Fujairah product stocks rose slightly but remain 65% below the 23 February level.
Australian gasoline and jet fuel cover fell by two days, and Singapore light and middle distillate stocks declined.
Middle Eastern crude futures rallied sharply as the prospect of prolonged Persian Gulf disruption grew. Dated Brent's premium to front-month futures rebounded on prompt physical tightness.
Investors lifted bullish Brent positions sharply while WTI net-long positioning was broadly unchanged.
The market's expectations of fundamentals over the next 6-12 months stay at the low end of an extremely tight 1.5-2.5 range, which supports current high crude prices.
China's imports are recovering and may offset higher Middle East flows. September imports were just over 9mb/d and weekly imports in October exceeded 9.5mb/d, against 11.5-12mb/d before the conflict.
China's crude refinery throughput hit a six-month high of 14mb/d in September. Onshore crude stock draws ran more than twice the May-August rate, which ANZ calls unsustainable in the medium term.
If China's renewed buying is more than opportunistic, ANZ expects it to keep markets tight and put upward pressure on oil prices.
Russian crude production is at a 23-year low of 8.5mb/d for a third straight month despite US sanctions relief. Russian seaborne crude exports are below 3.5mb/d in October, a 14-month low.
Tanker attacks reached an all-time high last week. An attack on a product tanker near Oman raises risks beyond Hormuz and to the ship-to-ship transfers sustaining regional exports.

sector_views.rationale: No equity stance is given. The tracker describes a physically tight market with limited buffers and prices highly sensitive to disruption, which is bullish for crude and diesel prices.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Fell for a fourth consecutive week and is trending lower, which limits supply availability.
Effective throughput is trending lower, limiting the market's ability to redirect barrels.

macro_indicators.indicator: Global distillate inventories vs five-year average
macro_indicators.interpretation: Points to product scarcity and continued refining stress.
Exceptionally high refining margins, broadly stable week on week at elevated levels.
No spare capacity can be delivered under prevailing conditions.
23-year low for a third straight month despite US sanctions relief.

macro_indicators.reading: just over 9mb/d in September, above 9.5mb/d weekly in October
macro_indicators.interpretation: Recovering but below the pre-conflict 11.5-12mb/d. Absorbs the increase in Persian Gulf exports.
Six-month high, accelerating draws on domestic crude stocks.

risk_factors: Further disruption to Persian Gulf production, trade flows or refinery operations, with little flexibility to absorb another shock.
A US bombing campaign after the 3 November midterms, or Israeli involvement.
Tanker attacks, now at an all-time high, spreading beyond Hormuz to ship-to-ship transfers.
Deepening refined product tightness as Persian Gulf shipping risks feed through.
Unsustainable drawdown of China's onshore crude stocks leading to either lower refinery runs or higher imports.
charts_described: The dashboard rates Persian Gulf exports at 14.3mb/d, Hormuz throughput at 60% of normal, distillate inventories at -4.9% vs 5y avg, diesel cracks at USD103.8/bbl and surplus OPEC capacity at 0mb/d, with an overall assessment of Vulnerable.
The Strait of Hormuz crossings chart shows the 7-day moving averages for outbound and inbound transits have fallen to zero.
The dark-fleet chart shows the 7-day moving average at just over two vessels per day.
vol_and_positioning: Investors increased bullish Brent bets, with the net-long position rising sharply last week.
WTI futures net-long positioning was broadly unchanged.
Dated Brent's premium to front-month futures rebounded after declines over recent weeks.
geopolitical: Media reports increasingly point to a likely US bombing campaign after the 3 November midterm elections.
President Trump has reiterated that a decision is looming on another wave of attacks or a deal with Iran.
Israel's involvement is being raised as Prime Minister Netanyahu faces domestic pressure ahead of a general election.
A possible summit between Russia, China and the US on the Middle East conflict has been raised in media, after an agreement to halt attacks on energy infrastructure failed to hold.
Houthi attacks on energy infrastructure are constraining Red Sea exports from Yanbu.
The US-Iran conflict began with an escalation in February 2026.
US sanctions relief on Russia has not lifted Russian output.

tension_points.bull_case: China is buying the additional Middle East crude leaving the Persian Gulf, with weekly imports above 9.5mb/d. If the buying is more than opportunistic, it keeps markets tight and pushes prices up.
tension_points.bear_case: China's stock draws are running at more than twice the May-August rate, which ANZ calls unsustainable. Refinery run rates could drop instead.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A drop in China's refinery run rates, or imports rising enough to rebuild stocks, would change the picture. ANZ names both as likely outcomes.

theme_stances.key_argument: Simultaneous supply and logistics constraints limit the market's ability to redirect barrels or absorb further disruption.
theme_stances.evidence: The dashboard therefore classifies the market as vulnerable.

theme_stances.key_argument: If China's renewed buying is more than opportunistic, it is likely to keep markets tight and upward pressure on oil prices.
theme_stances.evidence: likely to keep markets tight and upward pressure on oil prices
